extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent applicants/practioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and weighing objective/secondary evidence (unexpected results, commercial success, etc.) against a prima facie case of obviousness during patent examination/prosecution. Focuses on burdens, comparison standards, scope/commensurability, and required explanations by examiners and applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocking patent may discount secondary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A blocking patent can be evidence that discounts the significance of evidence that nobody but the blocking patent’s owners or licensees arrived at, developed, and marketed the invention covered by the later patent at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the blocking patent actually deterred activity is a fact‑specific inquiry; while record evidence of a blocking patent may be uncommon, examiners should be aware of its potential impact when evaluating secondary evidence. In any Office action, examiners should articulate why there is any discounting of the weight of the secondary consideration evidence when addressing the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh objective evidence against the prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: In making a final determination of patentability, evidence supporting patentability must be weighed against evidence supporting the prima facie case; the ultimate determination must be based on consideration of the entire record by a preponderance of the evidence, with due consideration to persuasiveness of arguments and secondary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission of objective evidence of patentability does not mandate a conclusion of patentability. The examiner must reconsider patentability when applicant timely traverses a rejection and base the decision on the whole record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate rebuttal evidence by facts, not only by attacking prima facie conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts established by rebuttal evidence must be evaluated along with the facts on which the conclusion of a prima facie case was reached, not assessed merely against the prima facie conclusion itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each piece of competent rebuttal evidence taken as a whole should be weighed against the evidence supporting the prima facie case; do not evaluate each item solely on its ability to 'knock down' the prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must explain discounting and assigned weights
rubrics_metrics.description: If, after evaluating the evidence, the examiner is not convinced the claimed invention is patentable, the next Office action should state that and identify the reason(s) (e.g., commercial success not convincing or not related to the technology). Any conclusion about whether evidence of obviousness outweighs objective evidence, along with any individual weights assigned to different objective indicia, should be explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear reasoning for discounting or assigning weight to secondary considerations; vague or ambiguous assignments of weight are defective (see Volvo Penta example where assigning 'some weight' without explanation was rejected). See MPEP § 2145 for guidance on sufficiency of rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness: difference in kind vs degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Any differences between the claimed invention and the prior art may be expected to result in some differences in properties; the issue is whether the properties differ to such an extent that the difference is really unexpected (a difference in kind rather than degree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases distinguish outcomes that are merely greater in degree (less persuasive) from those producing a new property dissimilar to the known property (more persuasive). Examiners should assess whether claimed properties are truly unexpected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater‑than‑expected results support nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A greater than expected result is an evidentiary factor pertinent to the legal conclusion of obviousness/nonobviousness of the claims at issue; synergistic (greater than additive) effects may be persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such effects are not necessarily sufficient by themselves — applicants must show results were greater than would have been expected from the prior art to an unobvious extent and that the results are of significant, practical advantage. Prior art teachings that would have led to an expectation of such effects can defeat the showing (e.g., mixtures expected to be greater than additive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority in a property shared with prior art can rebut obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unobvious or unexpected advantageous properties (e.g., superiority in a property the claimed compound shares with the prior art) can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No set number of examples is required; showing superiority against the closest prior art in relevant tests can be sufficient (see In re Chupp example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of an unexpected property is evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of a property not possessed by the prior art is evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes latent properties and additional advantages. However, submission of such evidence does not automatically require a finding of nonobviousness — weight and context matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of an expected property is evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of a property which a claimed invention would have been expected to possess based on prior art teachings is evidence of unobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claimed compounds expected to possess activity but do not, supporting nonobviousness. Consider whether prior art would have led one to expect the property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on applicant to establish unexpectedness and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence relied upon should establish that the differences in results are in fact unexpected and unobvious and of both statistical and practical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere conclusory statements in briefs or specifications are not entitled to weight; applicants must provide probative evidence showing magnitude and significance (statistical/practical) of unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant must explain proffered data/declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants have the burden of explaining the data in any declaration proffered as evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should expect detailed explanation tying the data to the claimed invention and why it rebuts the prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct and indirect comparative tests are probative if commensurate
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected properties may be in the form of a direct or indirect comparison of the claimed invention with the closest prior art which is commensurate in scope with the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both direct and indirect comparative testing can be sufficient; see cited cases for instances where indirect testing was upheld. Ensure comparisons are commensurate in scope with the claim limitations being tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate patentability by showing contributing cause in end product
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentability of an intermediate may be established by unexpected properties of an end product when one of ordinary skill would reasonably ascribe to the claimed intermediate the 'contributing cause' for such unexpectedly superior activity or property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must identify the cause of the unexpectedly superior activity/property in the end product and establish a nexus between the intermediate and the end product (i.e., show the intermediate is the contributing cause).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh expected and unexpected properties together
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected results must be weighed against evidence supporting a prima facie case of obviousness in making a final determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unexpected properties are not shown to have significance equal or greater than expected properties, they may not rebut obviousness. Conversely, expected beneficial results are evidence of obviousness. Evaluate the relative significance of each property (e.g., which effect is most significant to the claimed invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results must be commensurate in scope with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness must be commensurate in scope with the claims which the evidence is offered to support; the showing must be reviewed to see if results occur over the entire claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data limited to a narrow portion of a claimed range may be insufficient to support nonobviousness of the entire range (see examples where tests at certain temperatures or narrow % ranges failed to cover the claimed scope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species data may support genus/range nonobviousness when trend is extendable
rubrics_metrics.description: The nonobviousness of a genus or claimed range may be supported by data showing unexpected results of a species or narrower range if one of ordinary skill in the art would be able to determine a trend in the exemplified data which would allow reasonable extension of probative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If testing shows a trend that reasonably permits extrapolation to the broader claimed scope, species tests can be probative; isolated or unrepresentative species data without trend may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate criticality of a claimed range with sufficient tests
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish unexpected results over a claimed range, applicants should compare a sufficient number of tests both inside and outside the claimed range to show the criticality of the claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide multiple data points demonstrating a critical boundary or sharp change across the claimed versus unclaimed ranges (see In re Hill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit/declaration must compare with the closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must compare the claimed subject matter with the closest prior art to be effective to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed invention to disclosures of each cited reference to determine overlapping claim limitations and relative importance of limitations; deviations from references should be explained and evaluated; if unexplained and significant, require explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants may compare to prior art closer than examiner's reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may compare the claimed invention with prior art that is more closely related to the invention than the prior art relied upon by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons to closer art can provide stronger probative value for rebuttal; tests against closer analogs can be persuasive even if examiner cited different references.

rubrics_metrics.name: When two equally close references exist, tests must be sufficient for both
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing unexpected results over one of two equally close prior art references will not rebut a prima facie case unless the teachings of the references are sufficiently similar such that testing one would provide the same information as to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant tests less than all cited compounds, the test must be sufficient to permit a conclusion respecting the relative effectiveness of applicant’s claimed compounds and the compounds of the closest prior art; otherwise the evidence may be inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare only to closest subject matter that exists in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Although evidence of unexpected results must compare the claimed invention with the closest prior art, applicant is not required to compare with subject matter that does not exist in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require comparisons to hypothetical or non-existent prior art constructs; compare to the most relevant actual disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider advantages disclosed in or inherent from the totality of the record
rubrics_metrics.description: The totality of the record must be considered when determining whether a claimed invention would have been obvious; evidence and arguments directed to advantages not disclosed in the specification cannot be disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undisclosed but argued advantages or inherently flowing properties should be considered during prosecution (specification need not disclose proportions or values as critical for applicants to present evidence showing criticality). Examiners must consider such proffered evidence and arguments even if not in the original specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of production for commercial success and nexus on applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant asserting commercial success to support nonobviousness bears the burden of production in establishing commercial success and establishing a factually and legally sufficient nexus between the commercial success and the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO lacks means to gather evidence to support/refute assertions of commercial success and thus relies on the applicant to provide hard evidence. Evidence of commercial success for products not covered by the claims is not probative of nonobviousness.
